disclosure_text: I am a black/white mix individual. While I present as mostly white, the south african roots are part of my identity.
micronarrative:
I remember the trucker protests in Ottawa during the early days of the pandemic. It was a tense time, with a bunch of truckers parked outside the Parliament Buildings, exercising their right to protest. The media portrayed them as a bunch of angry, misguided individuals, but the reality was quite different. They were just a group of people who felt their livelihoods were being threatened and wanted to be heard.

On the other side, there were the RCMP officers, dressed in casual clothing, holding a Nazi flag. It was a bizarre and unsettling sight. The media, in their rush to condemn the truckers, completely ignored the actions of these officers. It made me question everything I thought I knew about journalism and the media's role in shaping public opinion.

The "no one is illegal" sign holders were a stark contrast. They were just holding signs and serving tea, trying to humanize the issue of undocumented immigration. Their approach was peaceful and respectful, yet the media often portrayed them as aggressive and demanding. It was frustrating to see such a stark difference in how different groups were represented.

That experience made me realize the importance of looking beyond the headlines and understanding the full context of events. It also made me less trusting of the media, as I saw firsthand how easily narratives can be skewed to fit a particular agenda.
